items.title: Mexico demands cleanup of suspected SpaceX rocket debris - The Texas Tribune
items.snippet: Mexican authorities say SpaceX must take responsibility for suspected rocket debris washing up on a beach near the Texas border, after a Starship booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico last week.
items.summary: A Texas Public Radio report by Stephania Corpi, published on the Texas Tribune at 18:39 CET on 23 November 2026, says Mexican authorities are calling on SpaceX to take responsibility for suspected rocket debris that began washing up Tuesday at Bagdad Beach near Matamoros, Tamaulipas, after the Starship booster from the 13 November test flight exploded over the Gulf of Mexico following an aborted catch. Environmental group Conibio Global says it has found at least 1,500 fragments of plastic, rubber and adhesive it believes came from the booster (its president, Jesús Elías Ibarra, says there are thousands), though the origin still needs confirming; Mexico’s environmental agency Profepa told the public not to touch the debris, and a dead Caguama turtle is being examined, while SpaceX said after similar debris last year that material tests found no chemical, biological or toxicological risks and that it wanted to work with Mexico on recovery.
items.timeSource: Texas Tribune byline, 11:39 a.m. Central

items.title: Britain says SpaceX restrictions in Ukraine 'dented confidence and trust' - Reuters
items.snippet: Britain's defence minister said on Monday that restrictions on the use of SpaceX's satellite communications by Ukraine's military have caused concern among European governments and damaged trust in the company's services.
items.summary: A Reuters report by Daniel Flynn, datelined Kyiv on 23 November 2026 and carried by Street Insider at 12:35 p.m. EST (18:35 CET) that day (the reuters.com page returned 401 here), says British defence minister Wes Streeting, visiting Kyiv, told journalists that restrictions on Ukraine’s military use of SpaceX satellite communications have been “a topic of conversation among defense ministers right across Europe” and “has really dented confidence and trust.” Ukraine said earlier this month that military units had seen significant disruptions to SpaceX’s Starshield system along the entire front line and in Russian-occupied areas; SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment, President Zelenskiy said Kyiv was talking with the US government and SpaceX to find the cause, and Streeting said allies are “owed a clear explanation about those service interruptions.”

items.title: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk's SpaceX over Grok AI's creation of child sexual abuse images - Reuters
items.snippet: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk's SpaceX over Grok AI's creation of child sexual abuse images Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters article by Diana Novak Jones, dated 23 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 15:50 CET that day (the Google News link was not opened; this is from the Reuters text syndicated on Yahoo Finance and Investing.com), says Virginia and Oregon have become the first states to sue Elon Musk’s SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp, alleging it profited from a Grok feature that produces child sexual abuse material and other non-consensual sexual images from photographs while failing to put safeguards in place, and that the company misled consumers about Grok’s safety while promoting “spicy mode.” The consumer-protection suits, filed in state courts, seek damages, penalties and court orders; SpaceX did not immediately comment, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones told Reuters that state attorneys general are stepping in amid limited federal AI regulation, and the piece notes SpaceX already faces more than a dozen individual lawsuits as well as a UK case by lawmaker Jess Asato.

items.title: Elon Musk Faces an A.I. Dilemma at SpaceX - The New York Times
items.snippet: Elon Musk Faces an A.I. Dilemma at SpaceX The New York Times
items.summary: A New York Times article by Grace Kay and Ryan Mac, listed in Google News at 17:13 CET on 23 November 2026 (the Google News and NYT pages could not be opened here; this is from Reuters/Investing.com and other contemporaneous reports of the Times piece), says SpaceX is making more money renting data-center compute to rivals — about $3.1 billion a month from Anthropic and about $800 million from Google, in contracts that could run through 2029 with 90 days’ notice — than from Grok, with the AI unit now generating more than half of company revenue. The Times reports Musk has told staff the company is falling behind in AI, briefly renamed an internal chat “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” and that SpaceX has shut down its AI companions initiative, shifted engineers off a Digital Optimus project, and disbanded a 60-person Grok Imagine team, while Musk told the paper’s DealBook conference that Anthropic is highly likely to keep renting and wants significantly more.

items.title: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims - CNBC
items.snippet: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims CNBC
items.summary: A CNBC article by Lora Kolodny, published at 13:40 CET on 23 November 2026, says Virginia and Oregon have become the first states to sue SpaceX over Grok, alleging the company failed to stop users from generating and sharing explicit deepfakes, including alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material, and falsely marketed Grok and X as generally safe. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones filed separate complaints in Multnomah County and Richmond seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, with Virginia also seeking consumer restitution; SpaceX did not immediately comment, and the suits were still pending the courts’ acceptance as of early Monday.

items.title: Jay Jones - Office of the Attorney General of Virginia
items.source: Office of the Attorney General of Virginia
items.snippet: Jay Jones Office of the Attorney General of Virginia
items.summary: A 23 November 2026 news release from Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones, listed in Google News at 13:17 CET that day, announces that Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield have filed consumer-protection suits against SpaceX — described as the parent of X, xAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence) and Grok — alleging the company failed to stop Grok from generating non-consensual sexual images and child sexual abuse material while promoting a “spicy mode” and falsely assuring users the tools were safe. Virginia’s case was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond and Oregon’s in Multnomah County Circuit Court; the release cites a CCDH estimate that Grok posted about three million sexualized images on X between 29 December 2025 and 8 January 2026, including about 23,000 that appeared to depict children, and says the attorneys general are seeking accountability and stronger consumer protections.

items.title: SpaceX shares can rally more than 60% from current levels, says Jefferies - CNBC
items.snippet: SpaceX shares can rally more than 60% from current levels, says Jefferies CNBC
items.summary: A CNBC article by Liz Napolitano, published at 13:01 CET on 23 November 2026, says Jefferies initiated coverage of SpaceX with a buy rating and a $210 price target, 64% above the last close, and that shares gained more than 3% after the call. Analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu called SpaceX’s engineering the foundation for durable growth in Space and Connectivity and exponential growth in Super Intelligence, and Jefferies said the company plans to have 2.5 to 3 gigawatts of compute online by the end of 2026; CNBC also notes that 34 of 44 analysts have a buy or strong buy, per LSEG, after shares fell more than 13% over the past month to below the $135 IPO price.

items.title: Aer Lingus brings ultra-fast, free Wi-Fi powered by Starlink to European flights - Aer Lingus
items.snippet: Aer Lingus has begun rolling out free Wi-Fi powered by Starlink on its short-haul fleet, with 29 short-haul aircraft expected to be equipped in early 2027.
items.summary: An Aer Lingus press release dated 23 November 2026 (the official page gives a date but no clock time) says the airline has begun rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi on its short-haul European fleet, starting with Airbus A320ceo EI-DVM in retro livery, with the service already available on select European flights and expected to extend across 29 short-haul aircraft in early 2027, beginning with destinations including Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Chief Customer Officer Susanne Carberry said the response on North American routes had been “fantastic,” and the airline said customers on its A330 long-haul fleet used an average of 1.8GB of data per connected device in October 2026.

items.title: Nvidia vs. SpaceX: Here's Which Stock I'd Put $1,000 Towards Right Now - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: Nvidia vs. SpaceX: Here's Which Stock I'd Put $1,000 Towards Right Now Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Motley Fool column by Chris Neiger, published at 3:18 a.m. ET (09:18 CET) on 23 November 2026 and listed in Google News via Yahoo Finance at 09:38 CET, says he would put $1,000 toward Nvidia rather than SpaceX because Nvidia is more profitable, spends less to grow, and is cheaper, with a forward P/E of around 10 versus SpaceX’s 49. He notes SpaceX’s Q3 2026 revenue jumped 161% to $14.6 billion and net income swung to $4.4 billion, but capex rose 185% to $19.6 billion and AI spending is set to be $35–40 billion in Q4 alone, while Nvidia’s sales more than doubled to $115.8 billion.

items.title: SpaceX launches 2 rockets from same pad 32 hours apart, smashing turnaround record (video) - Space
items.snippet: SpaceX launches 2 rockets from same pad 32 hours apart, smashing turnaround record (video) Space
items.summary: A Space.com article by Josh Dinner, last updated 23 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 05:06 CET that day, reports that Falcon 9 launched the classified NROL-136 mission for the National Reconnaissance Office from Vandenberg’s pad 4E at 13:23 CET on Sunday, 22 November, just 32 hours, 3 minutes and 21 seconds after USSF-317 lifted off from the same pad. It quotes SpaceX launch VP Kiko Dontchev saying this smashed the previous 45-hour record from Florida’s Pad 40 and that the next goal is a 24-hour turnaround, and notes it was the 15th launch for the NRO’s proliferated architecture and the 14th flight of booster B1097, which landed at Landing Zone 4.

items.title: NROL-136 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official NROL-136 mission page now confirms that Falcon 9 launched the NROL-136 mission at 4:23 a.m. PT on Sunday, 22 November 2026 from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. It says this was the 14th flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched Sentinel-6B, Twilight, NROL-172, Transporter-17, USSF-259 and eight Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the first stage landed on Landing Zone 4 at Vandenberg Space Force Base.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX NROL-136 mission page liftoff time (4:23 a.m. PT)

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers - Reuters
items.snippet: EXCLUSIVE: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters exclusive by Echo Wang and Milana Vinn, datelined New York on 22 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 12:03 CET that day (the Google News link returned 401; this is from the Reuters text syndicated on Yahoo Finance), says bankers privately complained that SpaceX tightly controlled its June IPO and kept financial and other information private, even as banks earned about half a billion dollars in fees. People close to that process told Reuters that Musk’s team instructed banks including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley on how to market the stock and to whom, specified order sizes to fill — in some cases a few billion dollars — and had banks underwrite the deal without being told what they would be paid; both SpaceX and Anthropic also negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on greenshoe overallotment shares.

items.title: CRS-35 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official CRS-35 mission page says that after 37 days docked to the International Space Station, Dragon completed its 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for NASA, splashing down off the coast of California on Saturday, 21 November 2026 at 2:04 p.m. PT. It says this was the fourth flight for this Dragon spacecraft, which previously flew CRS-26, CRS-29 and CRS-33, and that Falcon 9 had launched it to the station on Tuesday, 13 October at 6:33 a.m. ET from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX CRS-35 mission page splashdown time (2:04 p.m. PT)

items.title: SpaceX launches intelligence-gathering satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office - Spaceflight Now
items.snippet: SpaceX launches intelligence-gathering satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office Spaceflight Now
items.summary: Will Robinson-Smith at Spaceflight Now, in an article dated 21 November 2026, listed in Google News at 17:50 CET that day and updated at 8 a.m. EST on 22 November (14:00 CET), reports that SpaceX launched the NROL-136 mission for the National Reconnaissance Office on Sunday morning, sending an undisclosed number of intelligence-gathering satellites to low Earth orbit from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base — the fourth such proliferated-architecture launch this year and the 15th to date. The article says Falcon 9 first-stage booster B1097, making its 14th flight, lifted off at 4:23 a.m. PST (12:23 UTC), 32 hours, 3 minutes and 21 seconds after the prior USSF launch, smashing the Vandenberg pad turnaround record by more than 23 hours, and that the booster landed at Landing Zone 4 about 7.5 minutes after liftoff, the 38th landing at that site and the 680th Falcon booster landing to date.

items.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says - Space
items.snippet: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says Space
items.summary: A Space.com article by Mike Wall, published 21 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 14:00 CET that day, says Elon Musk told the TomorrowX Summit on Wednesday, 18 November, that Ship 42 — the first Starship upper stage SpaceX ever successfully recovered, caught at the Starbase tower after Flight 15 — will not fly again and will instead be left for public display because it is “kind of an historic ship,” even though he said it “could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment.” Wall writes that Musk did not say where the ship would be put on display, notes that SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy three times and reflown a booster twice but had never before attempted a Ship catch, and recalls Musk’s target of about 10,000 Starship missions a year by 2030.

items.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video) - Space
items.snippet: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video) Space
items.summary: A Space.com article by Mike Wall, published 21 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 06:28 CET that day, reports that SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force on a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base at 11:20 p.m. EST on 20 November (8:20 p.m. local / 04:20 GMT on 21 November), with first-stage booster B1100 landing about 8.5 minutes later on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific on its 11th flight. Wall notes that the payload and destination were not disclosed — SpaceX ended the webcast after the landing — though some experts think it may be Starshield satellites for the Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, and that this was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and SpaceX’s third Space Force mission in November.

items.title: USSF-317 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-317 page now confirms that Falcon 9 lifted off at 8:20 p.m. PT on 20 November 2026 from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. It says this was the 11th flight for the first-stage booster, which had previously launched NROL-105, USSF-385 and eight Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX “Liftoff!” post for USSF-317

items.title: SpaceX’s Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business - Ars Technica
items.snippet: SpaceX’s Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business Ars Technica
items.summary: An Ars Technica article by Eric Berger, listed in Google News at 23:16 CET on 20 November 2026, reports that Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX over Starshield disruptions in Ukraine. In a Friday letter to Elon Musk first reported by CNN, Himes asked SpaceX to explain the October 2026 Starshield changes and whether they were made unilaterally or directed by a U.S. official, writing that a “potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX.”

items.snippet: SPCX Stock Quote Price and Forecast CNN

items.title: Apollo, Goldman lead $44 billion SpaceX GPU debt financing - Reuters
items.snippet: Apollo, Goldman lead $44 billion SpaceX GPU debt financing Reuters
items.summary: The Reuters article itself returned 401 here; this summary is from the Reuters-bylined write-up carried by Investing.com and CNA, listed in Google News at 21:57 CET on 20 November 2026. It says Apollo and Goldman Sachs priced about $44 billion of senior and subordinated notes to fund GPUs and related equipment for SpaceX, which the firms called the largest GPU financing to date, an oversubscribed and upsized deal expected to finance Nvidia Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s terrestrial compute buildout, with leases starting when the equipment is delivered in the first half of 2027 and anchor commitments from BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR-advised accounts.

items.title: Trump intel chief warned no funding for Musk’s SpaceX without answers on Ukraine Starshield slowdown - CNN
items.snippet: Trump intel chief warned no funding for Musk’s SpaceX without answers on Ukraine Starshield slowdown CNN
items.summary: The CNN.com article itself could not be fetched here; this summary is from the CNN-bylined report by Zachary Cohen, Jennifer Hansler and Kylie Atwood, carried by KRDO and RNZ and listed in Google News at 19:09 CET on 20 November 2026. It says Rep. Jim Himes, who will become House Intelligence Committee chairman in January, warned in a classified message to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton that the committee “cannot authorize funds for the development of government systems that the government will not fully control,” seeking clarity on repeated slowdowns of Ukraine’s Starshield connection speed, and in a separate letter asked Elon Musk to explain the October 2026 Starshield service changes and whether they were made unilaterally by SpaceX or directed by a U.S. official, writing that a potentially unilateral contract modification and a lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight “calls into question every contract the US government has with SpaceX.”

items.title: SpaceX Falls 5%, Breaks Below IPO Price as Lenders Reportedly Balk at Musk’s Orbital AI Chip Plans; Rocket Lab Drops 3%, AST SpaceMobile Dips - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SpaceX Falls 5%, Breaks Below IPO Price as Lenders Reportedly Balk at Musk’s Orbital AI Chip Plans; Rocket Lab Drops 3%, AST SpaceMobile Dips Yahoo Finance
items.summary: The Yahoo Finance page behind this Google News link could not be opened here (it returned no article text); this summary is from the identically titled 24/7 Wall St. article by David Moadel, published at 9:52 a.m. ET on 20 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 15:52 CET that day. It says SpaceX stock was at $131.16, down 5% in morning trading and below its IPO price, adding to an 11% decline over the past month, after the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that lenders backing SpaceX’s debt package tried to restrict Elon Musk from launching the Nvidia chips securing the financing into space — fearing they could not recover and sell the chips if SpaceX defaulted — and that it was unclear whether those restrictions made it into the final agreement; Bloomberg, the article adds, reported SpaceX raised $32 billion in bonds as part of a $40 billion financing package including bank loans, arranged by Goldman Sachs with Apollo Global Management and with PIMCO among the buyers, to fund a five-year lease of Nvidia processors, with the largest tranche paying a yield well above the average for U.S. investment-grade corporate bonds, while Rocket Lab fell 3% to $49.67 and AST SpaceMobile fell 1% to $25.18.

items.title: Three Ways SpaceX Stock Can Buck the AI Slump - Barron's
items.snippet: Three Ways SpaceX Stock Can Buck the AI Slump Barron's
items.summary: A Barron’s article by Al Root, listed in Google News at 12:55 CET on 20 November 2026, says SpaceX stock “feels tethered to its $135 IPO price” and is failing to achieve escape velocity. The rest of the article is behind a paywall here (Barron’s returned 401; Yahoo Finance only showed that lede), so this summary is limited to the headline and opening line.

items.title: SpaceX - Britannica
items.snippet: SpaceX Britannica
items.summary: The Google News link and the main Britannica page were blocked; Britannica’s Scholars encyclopedia entry by Alison Eldridge describes SpaceX as an American aerospace company founded by Elon Musk in 2002, now headquartered in Starbase, Texas, and covers Falcon, Dragon, Starlink and Starship plus the February 2026 xAI acquisition, a June 2026 IPO of 555.6 million shares at $135 that raised $75 billion and valued the company at about $1.77 trillion, and the August 2026 $60 billion purchase of Cursor. It says that as of June 2026 Starlink had more than 10,200 satellites in orbit and 12 million subscribers, and that after the xAI deal SpaceX made artificial intelligence one of its three main business segments alongside space and connectivity.

items.title: SpaceX launches satellites for the U.S. Space Force’s data network constellation - Spaceflight Now
items.snippet: SpaceX launches satellites for the U.S. Space Force’s data network constellation Spaceflight Now
items.summary: Will Robinson-Smith at Spaceflight Now, in an article updated at 11:45 p.m. EDT on 20 November 2026 (05:45 CET on 21 November), reports that SpaceX launched USSF-317, a classified U.S. Space Force mission carrying an undisclosed number of satellites, on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg at 8:20 p.m. PST (05:20 CET on 21 November), after scrubbing Thursday night without stating a reason. Booster B1100, on its 11th flight, landed a little more than eight minutes after liftoff on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship, the 235th landing on that vessel and the 679th Falcon booster landing to date.

items.title: How to Invest In SpaceX (SPCX) — And How Not To - NerdWallet
items.snippet: How to Invest In SpaceX (SPCX) — And How Not To NerdWallet
items.summary: NerdWallet explains how a retail investor can buy SPCX now that SpaceX is public — and how someone who does not want the stock might still end up with exposure through funds — after the 12 Jun IPO at $135 that raised about $75 billion at a $1.75 trillion opening valuation. The guide recalls a first-day close a little above $160 and a brief spike above $225, followed by a bumpier trade often below the offer price; it is an explainer, not a recommendation.

items.title: Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX - Al Jazeera
items.snippet: Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX Al Jazeera
items.summary: An Al Jazeera article by Hanna Duggal, published 19 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 08:44 CET that day, says Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, pricing shares at $83 for a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, after selling 980 million shares (up from a planned 825 million) above a $70–$78 range on six-times oversubscription, with trading due to start on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. It says Anthropic overtook SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June at $135 a share and a $1.75 trillion valuation, a total that rose to $85.7 billion after extra shares were sold, and it recaps Anthropic’s $33.2 billion of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, a $104 billion net loss largely from non-cash adjustments, and nearly $901 billion of computing and infrastructure commitments.

items.title: USSF-380 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-380 mission page says the company is targeting Saturday, 28 November 2026 for a Falcon 9 launch from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, with a four-hour window opening at 8:39 p.m. PT and a backup at 6:26 p.m. PT on Sunday, 29 November. It says this will be the 27th flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched USSF-62, OneWeb Launch 20, NROL-145, Transporter-18 and 22 Starlink missions, that after stage separation the first stage will land on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, and that a live webcast will begin about 10 minutes prior to liftoff on the site and on X @SpaceX.
items.timeSource: Google News first listing of the official SpaceX mission page

items.title: USSF-380 Mission - SpaceX
items.snippet: USSF-380 Mission SpaceX
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-380 page, listed in Google News at 17:35 CET on 18 November 2026, says the company is targeting Friday 27 November for a Falcon 9 launch from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, with a four-hour window opening at 8:53 p.m. PT and a backup at 8:39 a.m. PT on Saturday 28 November. It says this will be the 27th flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched USSF-62, OneWeb Launch 20, NROL-145, Transporter-18 and 22 Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster will land on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific, with a possible sonic boom in Santa Barbara, San Luis Obispo and Ventura counties.

items.title: How the Anthropic IPO stacks up against SpaceX - Reuters
items.snippet: How the Anthropic IPO stacks up against SpaceX Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters article by Niket Nishant, dated 18 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 16:52 CET that day, compared the then-upcoming Anthropic IPO with SpaceX’s June debut, saying Anthropic was expected to be the second-biggest U.S. offering on record and that a $1.4 trillion valuation then discussed by bankers would be about 40 times trailing 12-month sales, versus roughly 92 times revenue when SpaceX went public at about $1.8 trillion. The live Reuters page could not be fetched here; this summary is from a Reuters-bylined syndication, which also noted SpaceX’s tighter lock-up for Elon Musk, who is barred from selling for a year, and that SpaceX shares were trading above their IPO price but below the June open.

items.title: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure - NASA (.gov)
items.snippet: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure NASA (.gov)
items.summary: A NASA news release by Lauren E. Low, dated 17 November 2026 and updated on 18 and 19 November, listed in Google News at 20:17 CET on 17 November, says NASA will cover the departure of the SpaceX Dragon on the 35th commercial resupply mission, with undocking from Harmony’s space-facing port no earlier than 12:05 p.m. EST on Friday 20 November and live coverage from 11:45 a.m., targeting splashdown off the California coast at about 4:55 p.m. EST (1:55 p.m. PST) on Saturday 21 November, weather permitting. It says the spacecraft arrived on 15 October after a Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral two days earlier with more than 6,300 pounds of cargo, and that thousands of pounds are coming back, including a 3D-bioprinted blood-vessel construct, frozen tumor organoids, microbial samples and a lighting system that spent more than three years on station.

items.title: SPCX Stock In Focus: SpaceX To Reportedly Launch $4B Bond Sale This Week - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SPCX Stock In Focus: SpaceX To Reportedly Launch $4B Bond Sale This Week Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Yahoo Finance article by Arnab Paul, listed in Google News at 19:07 CET on 17 November 2026, cites a Bloomberg report that SpaceX could begin selling around $4 billion of bonds that week as the first part of a $40 billion financing plan to buy Nvidia Vera Rubin chips, with Goldman Sachs and Apollo expected to underwrite the sale and BlackRock and KKR funds also having made financing commitments. It says a special-purpose company managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP would buy the chips and lease them to SpaceX for five years, a structure designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX’s balance sheet and protect its investment-grade ratings, and that SpaceX had not responded to a request for comment.

items.title: Why SpaceX Stock Is Down After Its Historic Starship Catch - Barron's
items.snippet: Why SpaceX Stock Is Down After Its Historic Starship Catch Barron's
items.summary: A Barron’s article by Al Root and Callum Keown, listed in Google News at 17:53 CET on 16 November 2026 under the headline “Why SpaceX Stock Is Down After Its Historic Starship Catch,” says SpaceX did something amazing on Saturday but the stock is barely budging on Monday, after Starship’s upper stage came back from orbit and was caught by the launch tower’s mechanical arms, which the writers call an amazing feat of engineering. The rest of the article could not be fetched here because of the paywall.

items.title: SpaceX's Starship feat should remind investors that the company at its 'core' is a rocket builder - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SpaceX's Starship feat should remind investors that the company at its 'core' is a rocket builder Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Yahoo Finance article by Pras Subramanian, published at 16:16 CET on 16 November 2026, says SpaceX caught Starship’s upper stage for the first time on Saturday after Flight 15 deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and cites Evercore ISI’s Kutgun Maral saying the mission should remind investors the company is at its “core” a rocket builder, because long-term value will be decided more by the cost and frequency of access to orbit than by the next gigawatt of compute or contract renewal. It also quotes William Blair’s Louie DiPalma calling the Super Heavy booster abort, which Musk attributed to being slightly low on fuel, a “footnote in an otherwise historic mission,” and contrasts that with ULA’s Vulcan anomaly on Sunday that lost all 40 Amazon Leo satellites.

items.title: SpaceX achieves another historic first - The Economist
items.snippet: SpaceX achieves another historic first The Economist
items.summary: An Economist Science and Technology article, listed in Google News at 12:33 CET on 15 November 2026, says that on 14 November, during Starship’s 15th test flight, SpaceX caught the rocket’s second stage at its launch tower for the first time, having previously caught boosters mid-air but never the upper half. The Economist page itself returned 403 here; the visible opening says that leaves the company on the cusp of building the first fully reusable rocket, which should cut the cost of reaching space further.

items.title: SpaceX Starship returns to landing pad from orbit, acing test for reusable rockets - Reuters
items.snippet: SpaceX Starship returns to landing pad from orbit, acing test for reusable rockets Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters report by Joey Roulette, listed in Google News at 22:40 CET on 14 November 2026, says Starship returned from a 22-hour voyage in orbit and descended for the first time into the Mechazilla arms at the Texas tower it launched from a day earlier, after the Super Heavy booster failed to make a similar return about 10 minutes after Friday’s liftoff. The piece says the ship had deployed 26 Starlink satellites, completed 14 orbits over 22.5 hours, and that Elon Musk and SpaceX engineers began inspecting Ship 42 within hours of the catch.

items.title: SpaceX Catches Starship From Orbit for the First Time. Here’s What It Means for Starlink’s Costs - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SpaceX Catches Starship From Orbit for the First Time. Here’s What It Means for Starlink’s Costs Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Yahoo Finance report by Gian Estrada, syndicated from TIKR and listed in Google News at 14:21 CET on 15 November 2026, says SpaceX caught Ship 42 with the launch tower for the first time on 14 November, about 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off — after 14 orbits and the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites — while the Super Heavy booster catch was called off after a fuel-system problem and the booster exploded before reaching the Gulf of Mexico. Estrada argues a returning ship is what would turn Starship’s much larger capacity into cheaper Starlink launches (SpaceX was its own biggest customer, with 75% of the mass it put in orbit in the third quarter), but treats Saturday as proof the hardware works, not yet proof costs come down, until a caught ship flies again quickly.

items.title: ‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters - Al Jazeera
items.snippet: ‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters Al Jazeera
items.summary: An Al Jazeera report by Priyanka Shankar, listed in Google News at 15:14 CET on 15 November 2026, explains why Saturday’s mid-air catch matters: after 14 orbits and about 22.5 hours, Starship slipped into the Mechazilla “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase — the first capture of a Starship upper stage, which engineers say is a step toward fully reusable mega-rockets. The piece quotes SpaceX commentator Dan Huot calling it “the holy grail of spaceflight,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman describing it as “almost magic,” and notes that Elon Musk and engineers said Ship 42, including its heat shield, appeared to have worked well.

items.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch? - Space
items.snippet: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch? Space
items.summary: A Space.com report by Mike Wall, listed in Google News at 12:00 CET on 15 November 2026, asks what comes next after Flight 15: the Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown after a low-fuel alarm, but the Ship upper stage was caught at Starbase 22.5 hours after liftoff — a first, while Super Heavy has been caught on three prior tests. Wall writes that SpaceX has yet to show rapid reflight of either stage (Ship has never been reused; Super Heavy has been reflown twice, months apart), that Musk wants both stages reused and has talked of 10,000 Starship launches a year by 2030, and that remaining hurdles include orbital refueling and a crew cabin for NASA’s Artemis IV lunar landing, targeted for 2028.

items.title: SpaceX pulls off first-ever spaceship 'catch' - AFP.com
items.snippet: SpaceX pulls off first-ever spaceship 'catch' AFP.com
items.summary: An AFP report, listed in Google News at 00:04 CET on 15 November 2026, says SpaceX on Saturday pulled off the first-ever catch of a spaceship when Starship emerged from the clouds after re-entry and slipped between the mechanical chopstick arms above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase in south Texas, a feat spokesman Dan Huot called the “Holy Grail of spaceflight.” The article notes it was the 15th test flight of the world’s biggest rocket, that the ship orbited Earth 14 times and deployed 26 Starlink satellites during a 22-hour journey, that SpaceX had previously caught returning boosters three times, and that the Super Heavy booster hit a technical issue on Friday and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico instead of being caught.

items.title: Starship Flight 15
items.summary: SpaceX’s official Starship Flight 15 page says the vehicle lifted off from Pad 2 at Starbase on 13 November 2026, reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, while the Super Heavy booster aborted its catch after a boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass and was diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf, where its flight termination system was triggered after the landing burn. After more than 20 hours in space and a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the same launch site 22.5 hours after liftoff and, for the first time, was caught by Mechazilla’s arms.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX post linking the Flight 15 recap

items.title: Starship Flight 15 - SpaceX
items.snippet: Starship Flight 15 SpaceX
items.summary: SpaceX’s official Starship Flight 15 page, listed in Google News at 09:00 CET on 13 November 2026, says the vehicle lifted off from Pad 2 at Starbase on 13 November 2026, reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, while the Super Heavy booster aborted its catch after a boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass and was diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf, where its flight termination system was triggered after the landing burn. After more than 20 hours in space and a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the same launch site 22.5 hours after liftoff and, for the first time, was caught by Mechazilla’s arms.

items.title: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first - CNBC
items.snippet: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first CNBC
items.summary: A CNBC report by Lora Kolodny, published at 22:14 CET on 14 November 2026 and later updated, says SpaceX successfully caught the upper-stage spacecraft of Starship from orbit with the launch tower’s “chopsticks” at Starbase, Texas, after the vehicle flew around the Earth 14 times. The piece notes that on Friday SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, diverting it to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown where it exploded before hitting the water, and that Flight 15 also released another 26 of SpaceX’s newest Starlink v3 satellites.

items.title: SpaceX Catches a Starship - Space Policy Online
items.snippet: SpaceX Catches a Starship Space Policy Online
items.summary: A SpacePolicyOnline report by Marcia Smith, listed at 22:53 CET on 14 November 2026, says Starship’s 15th integrated flight test returned after 14 orbits and was caught at the Starbase launch tower, the first attempt to catch the second stage after an orbital mission, after SpaceX had previously caught Super Heavy boosters on three flights. The piece says the booster did not return as planned after the guidance system diverted it to the Gulf, that IFT-15 deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and that this was Booster 22 and Starship 42 (S42).

items.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video) - Space
items.snippet: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video) Space
items.summary: A Space.com report by Mike Wall, listed at 23:04 CET on 14 November 2026, says SpaceX caught Starship’s upper stage for the first time on 14 November, with Ship 42 nestling into Mechazilla’s arms at 4:20 p.m. EST, about 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off, while the Super Heavy booster had diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown after a low-fuel alarm. The article quotes SpaceX’s Dan Huot calling the catch “the holy grail of spaceflight,” and notes Flight 15 again deployed 26 next-gen Starlink V3 satellites.

items.title: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history - NPR
items.snippet: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history NPR
items.summary: An NPR report posted at 22:42 CET on 14 November 2026 says Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday and was caught in midair by giant mechanical arms after a 22-hour flight, the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space, though the company fell short of a double catch after the first-stage booster exploded following Friday’s liftoff. The piece says the upper stage reached orbit, released 26 advanced Starlink satellites, completed 14 laps of Earth, and that SpaceX’s Kate Tice said the booster’s engines stopped firing too soon, after which its guidance system initiated a watery detour and self-destruction.

items.title: SpaceX deploys Starlink satellites in Starship test, but booster crashes into Gulf - NPR
items.snippet: SpaceX deploys Starlink satellites in Starship test, but booster crashes into Gulf NPR
items.summary: An NPR Weekend Edition Saturday interview with Geoff Brumfiel, listed at 13:40 CET on 14 November 2026 and recorded before the catch attempt, says Friday night’s Starship test reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, but the Super Heavy booster that was supposed to land at Starbase instead crashed into the Gulf of Mexico. Brumfiel said the plan later that day was for the ship to reenter, fly back to Starbase and be grabbed by the launch tower’s mechanical arms, a step he described as essential to making Starship rapidly reusable for Starlink and orbital data centers.

items.title: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world - Ars Technica
items.snippet: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world Ars Technica
items.summary: An Ars Technica report by Eric Berger, listed in Google News at 01:40 CET on 15 November 2026, describes Starship’s upper stage returning to Starbase on Saturday, flipping from horizontal to vertical as three Raptor engines ignited, and being snagged by the launch-tower arms — a hugely significant step, he writes, toward a massive, rapidly reusable rocket after earlier practice runs into the Indian Ocean. Berger notes SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship to the tower as a proof of concept, currently builds an upper stage every three weeks at the South Texas Starfactory (sized for one every three days), and says the heat shield is likely the hardest part of making such landings routine.

items.title: SpaceX makes history with Starship catch - NPR
items.snippet: SpaceX makes history with Starship catch NPR
items.summary: An NPR All Things Considered segment by Geoff Brumfiel and Rob Schmitz, listed at 23:31 CET on 14 November 2026, describes SpaceX catching Starship as it returned from orbit at Starbase, with the ship reentering, bursting through clouds, flipping vertical and being grabbed by Mechazilla’s arms. Brumfiel notes the flight also deployed 26 Starlink satellites, that rapid reuse still requires bringing both the booster and ship back, and that Friday’s Super Heavy booster aborted and self-destructed in the Gulf.

items.title: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas - The New York Times
items.snippet: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas The New York Times
items.summary: The New York Times page itself could not be fetched here; a syndicated reprint of Kenneth Chang’s Times report, listed in Google News at 01:36 CET on 15 November 2026, says Starship returned from orbit on Saturday afternoon and was caught between the mechanical “chopstick” arms on the South Texas launch tower — the first time an upper stage had been brought back from orbit, on the first try. The 15th test flight launched Friday afternoon and deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites, while the planned Super Heavy booster catch — which would have been a first double-catch — did not happen, and the article notes that showing the heat shield and engines can be reused quickly is still further off.

items.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launchpad arms in a dramatic first - NBC News
items.snippet: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launchpad arms in a dramatic first NBC News
items.summary: An NBC News report by Reuters and Evan Bush, first published on 13 November 2026 and updated at 22:33 CET on 14 November, says SpaceX caught its Starship spacecraft with giant mechanical arms at its South Texas launch site on Saturday, recovering the upper stage for the first time after nearly a day in orbit. The catch capped Starship’s 15th test flight; the company had planned to catch both stages, but the Super Heavy booster was diverted offshore after Friday’s liftoff and exploded a short distance over the Gulf of Mexico.

items.title: Restoring Boca Chica Beach
items.summary: SpaceX’s 13 November Updates post, titled “Restoring Boca Chica Beach,” says the company has discussed buying about 1,200 acres of Texas Parks and Wildlife land surrounding the Starbase launch facility, with more than half to be permanently protected under a conservation easement, and states clearly that Boca Chica Beach is not part of the proposal and will remain public. It argues the land is largely mudflats and fragile dunes with limited recreation, that securing the perimeter would improve public safety around the launch site, and that sale proceeds would let Texas invest in new parkland in the Rio Grande Valley, while SpaceX commits to permanently conserve about 600 acres and continues beach cleanups and sea-turtle work.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX post linking the 13 November Updates item

items.title: SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster malfunction thwarts double catch attempt - PBS
items.snippet: SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster malfunction thwarts double catch attempt PBS
items.summary: A PBS NewsHour piece by Marcia Dunn of the Associated Press, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX’s attempt to recover the entire Starship stack at the pad was thwarted when Super Heavy v3 Booster 22 malfunctioned, automatically aborted, and ended up exploding after being diverted to the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship 42 spacecraft still reached orbit. It says this was the first catch attempt for the upgraded 236-foot booster and that, barring further trouble, the ship will try a first-ever return-from-orbit catch Saturday after about 22 hours and 15 laps at roughly 170 miles (275 kilometers), having prepared to deploy 26 of SpaceX’s most advanced Starlink satellites.

items.title: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust - NPR
items.snippet: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust NPR
items.summary: An NPR report by Geoff Brumfiel, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX plans its most ambitious Starship test later today — lift off from South Texas, orbit Earth, and land vertically at the same pad 22 and a half hours later — and that experts warn the shift toward Starship could strand NASA, because SpaceX has said it will stop flying Falcon 9, which launches Dragon, currently the only American spacecraft that can ferry NASA astronauts to and from the ISS. NASA has contracted three additional ISS flights that would only take Dragon through 2028 if flown every six months with no further orders; SpaceX did not comment, its latest report showed about $2.1 billion of launch revenue through September versus $12.8 billion from Starlink and $10.9 billion from AI, and Gwynne Shotwell suggested Boeing’s problem-plagued Starliner (next crewed flight sometime in 2028) could take some of that NASA business.

items.title: SpaceX faces key launch test tonight with 'double catch' of Starship and Super Heavy Booster - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SpaceX faces key launch test tonight with 'double catch' of Starship and Super Heavy Booster Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Yahoo Finance article by Pras Subramanian, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX’s Starship Flight 15 is scheduled for Friday night at 5:45 p.m. ET and will attempt a first-time “double catch” of both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage at Boca Chica, which the company said would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system, while also deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites that SpaceX says add 1 terabit of capacity each — about equal to ten Falcon 9 V2 Mini launches. Morgan Stanley’s Adam Jonas called the flight “one of the most significant catalysts in SpaceX’s 20+ year history”; the piece notes the stock was up 2% for the week after trading between $148.44 and $135.40, and cites Bloomberg reporting that a SpaceX–Tesla merger could be announced as early as December or slip into early 2027.

items.title: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket - CNBC
items.snippet: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket CNBC
items.summary: A CNBC report by Lora Kolodny, published 13 November 2026, says Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 4:47 p.m. local time (5:47 p.m. ET) after FAA launch authorization, but SpaceX aborted the plan to catch and reuse the booster and diverted it to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown, where it burst into flames. The upper stage continued to orbit for a planned 14 trips around Earth and a Saturday landing back at Starbase; Kolodny notes the flight also deployed another 26 Starlink V3 satellites, that William Blair analysts said even a failed catch and a delay of a few months would not be that consequential, and that SpaceX faces fresh criticism over Starshield restrictions in Ukraine.

items.title: SpaceX’s Starship Just Did Something for Only the 2nd Time. Saturday Could Be Even Bigger. - Yahoo Finance
items.snippet: SpaceX’s Starship Just Did Something for Only the 2nd Time. Saturday Could Be Even Bigger. Yahoo Finance
items.summary: A Motley Fool article by Johnny Rice, dated 13 November 2026 and listed in Google News under Yahoo Finance, says Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47 p.m. ET, reached orbit at 6:13 p.m. ET — only the second time Starship has done so — and began deploying 26 Starlink satellites, while the Super Heavy booster was diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown and burst into flames. Rice notes SpaceX has not shared details of the booster issue, that a catch of the upper stage is scheduled for 4:17 p.m. ET on Saturday only if systems stay healthy, and that the Space segment was just $1.8 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue.

items.title: SpaceX launches 15th Starship flight with hopes of achieving first round trip - Reuters
items.snippet: SpaceX launches 15th Starship flight with hopes of achieving first round trip Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters report by Joey Roulette, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX’s 15th Starship flight was scheduled to lift off at 4:45 p.m. CT from Starbase and will try for the first time to catch the upper stage at the Texas launch site rather than ditching it in the ocean, after also returning the Super Heavy booster — a mission that would also be the rocket’s second to deploy operational Starlink satellites. SpaceX secured its FAA launch license hours before the planned liftoff; if the plan holds, the booster would be caught and then moved off the pad so the ship can return after about 22 hours and 14 orbits, with the debut ship catch around 2:45 p.m. CT on Saturday.

items.title: Starship Flight 15 puts SpaceX’s moonshots to the test - Scientific American
items.snippet: Starship Flight 15 puts SpaceX’s moonshots to the test Scientific American
items.summary: A Scientific American article by Lee Billings, dated 13 November 2026 and updated later that day, says Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47 p.m. EST with Ship 42, aiming to catch both the Super Heavy booster and, for the first time, the orbiter after about 14 orbits, but the booster diverted to an offshore splashdown after engine trouble. Ship 42 reached orbit and deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites, with a return to Starbase planned around 4:15 p.m. EST on 14 November; the piece frames the flight as a reusability test needed for Starlink, orbital data centers, and NASA’s Artemis lander work.

items.title: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX - Space
items.snippet: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX Space
items.summary: A Space.com article by Andrew Jones, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX is targeting today for Starship Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the Ship upper stage as well as the Super Heavy booster, which the company calls the “Holy Grail of rocketry” — with a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST, a first catch of a next-gen Super Heavy V3 about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, and, if conditions are met, a Ship catch back at Starbase about 21 hours later after deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Jones writes that a successful double catch would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system, a step toward the roughly 10,000 Starship launches a year SpaceX is targeting by 2030, and quotes Elon Musk saying that if both catches succeed it will mark the first time all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact — “the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary.”

items.title: [2026-11-13] Ranking Member Shaheen, Senator Coons Demand Elon Musk... - U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (.gov)
items.source: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (.gov)
items.snippet: [2026-11-13] Ranking Member Shaheen, Senator Coons Demand Elon Musk... U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (.gov)
items.summary: A 13 November 2026 Senate Foreign Relations Committee press release, listed in Google News at 12:07 CET on 14 November, says Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) sent a letter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk demanding that he and SpaceX preserve documents and communications about disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield access, and confirm those preservation steps in writing by 30 November. The senators wrote that restrictions from 13–24 October 2026, and a renewed Starshield disruption reported by President Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military on 12 November, impaired Ukrainian air defenses, and they pointed to conflicting accounts from Musk, Defense Secretary Hegseth and Secretary of State Rubio about who ordered the limits.

items.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video) - Space
items.snippet: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video) Space
items.summary: A Space.com report by Josh Dinner, published 13 November 2026 and updated at 7:10 p.m. ET after successful payload deployment, says Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47 p.m. ET and that SpaceX called off the Super Heavy booster catch, bringing it down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch for reasons that were not immediately clear. The story says Ship reached orbit for only the second time, at about 170 miles (275 kilometers), deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and that a first-ever Ship catch was planned for Saturday at about 4:17 p.m. EST if systems stayed healthy.

items.title: Building the future — Starbase and Cochise County supercompute investments
items.summary: SpaceX’s 12 November 2026 Updates post says it is advancing two supercompute projects — a facility at Starbase in the Rio Grande Valley and a campus in Cochise County, Arizona — that together represent more than $74 billion in planned U.S. investment. It plans more than $24 billion of new supercomputing at Starbase (on top of more than $15 billion already invested there), with the site generating its own power, plus $220 million to expand Brownsville’s water and wastewater capacity by 20 million gallons a day, and a roughly $50 billion Arizona campus expected to support about 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, using dry cooling with no planned industrial groundwater use.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX posts linking the 12 November Updates item

items.title: From SpaceX to Anthropic, markets have a new playbook for mega-share debuts - Reuters
items.snippet: From SpaceX to Anthropic, markets have a new playbook for mega-share debuts Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters analysis by Vidya Ranganathan, dated 12 Nov 2026, says Anthropic’s expected IPO next week is likely to follow SpaceX’s June debut, in which faster index inclusion by providers such as Nasdaq drew a large pool of passive buying in the first 15 days. It notes SpaceX shares were up 50% by day 3 from a $150 opening-day debut and stayed above the $135 IPO price for the first 15 days, before drifting lower ahead of lock-up expirations, and that Anthropic is similarly offering only about 6% of outstanding shares.

items.title: SpaceX plans over $74 billion investment in Texas, Arizona AI campuses - Reuters
items.snippet: SpaceX plans over $74 billion investment in Texas, Arizona AI campuses Reuters
items.summary: A Reuters report dated 12 November 2026 says SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion in two supercomputing campuses — more than $24 billion at Starbase in Texas and roughly $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona — expanding an AI business that already generated more than half of third-quarter revenue. The Arizona campus still needs county approval and faces a 2,400-signature petition ahead of a December public hearing, while a Starbase city notice describes a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility on about 444 acres, with the City Commission due to consider a property tax abatement on 9 December.

items.title: USSF-627 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-627 page now confirms that Falcon 9 lifted off at 8:36 p.m. PT on 11 November 2026 from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. It says this was the seventh flight for the first-stage booster, which had previously launched NROL-179, SDA-T1TL-E, SDA-T1TL-A and three Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX “Liftoff!” post for USSF-627

items.title: USSF-627 Mission - SpaceX
items.snippet: USSF-627 Mission SpaceX
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-627 mission page confirms that Falcon 9 lifted off at 8:36 p.m. PT on 11 November 2026 from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. It says this was the seventh flight for the first-stage booster, which had previously launched NROL-179, SDA-T1TL-E, SDA-T1TL-A and three Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.

items.title: USSF-266 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official USSF-266 mission page says the company is targeting Tuesday, 24 November 2026 for a Falcon 9 launch from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, with a four-hour window opening at 7:55 a.m. PT and a backup at 7:46 a.m. PT on Wednesday, 25 November. It says this will be the 29th flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched Crew-7, CRS-29, PACE, Transporter-10, EarthCARE, NROL-186, Transporter-13, TRACERS, NROL-48, COSMO-SkyMED Second Generation FM3, USSF-153, USSF-481 and 16 Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the first stage will land on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.
items.timeSource: Google News first listing of the official SpaceX mission page

items.title: USSF-432 mission
items.summary: This is SpaceX’s official page for USSF-432, a Falcon 9 mission from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. Company posts show liftoff on 7 Nov 2026 and a first-stage landing on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship; the webpage itself is a JavaScript launch page and returned no extra article text here.
items.timeSource: Official SpaceX “Liftoff!” post for USSF-432

items.title: 8-K — Item 5.02, departure of a director or officer
items.timeSource: EDGAR filing index: accepted 2026-11-06 16:15:01 ET
items.summary: The 8-K reports that Donald Harrison, a Class B director, resigned from the SpaceX board effective 4 Nov 2026, and that the resignation was not because of any disagreement on operations, policies, or practices. An IR note the same day thanks Harrison, who had served since February 2015 and is President of Global Partnerships and Corporate Development at Google.

items.title: 8-K — Item 8.01, Apollo GPU finance-lease commitment
items.timeSource: EDGAR filing index: accepted 2026-10-26 08:00:18 ET
items.summary: The 8-K says that on 24 Oct 2026 SpaceX signed a binding commitment for a master finance lease with an Apollo-managed lessor that will buy GPU pods and related equipment and lease them to SpaceX. The company expects about $40 billion of principal payments over roughly five-year tranche schedules, with closing targeted by year-end 2026 and deliveries in the first half of 2027; an IR release adds that the chips are next-generation NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and that Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and KKR also committed.

items.title: S-8 — Cursor reoffer prospectus / S-8
items.timeSource: EDGAR header ACCEPTANCE-DATETIME 20261022162430 (16:24:30 ET)
items.summary: SpaceX filed a Form S-8 with a reoffer prospectus so shares issued in the Cursor acquisition can be resold by employees and other service providers, subject to Rule 144 and any lock-ups. The live EDGAR document could not be fetched here (403); contemporaneous descriptions of this filing put the registered reoffer amount at about 23.6 million Class A shares.

items.title: SpaceX reports third quarter 2026 results
items.summary: SpaceX’s official third-quarter 2026 release reports revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from $5.6 billion a year earlier, with net income of $4.4 billion and Adjusted EBITDA of $8.8 billion. Super Intelligence revenue was $7.56 billion and Connectivity $5.25 billion, with 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers and $69 monthly ARPU; the company also completed its first revenue Starship mission, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites.
items.timeSource: EDGAR acceptance of the Q3 2026 earnings 8-K (the press release is the 8-K exhibit)

items.title: NG-25 mission
items.summary: SpaceX’s official NG-25 mission page says the company is targeting Sunday, 29 November 2026 for a Falcon 9 launch of Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL commercial resupply mission (NG-25) to the International Space Station from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, with liftoff targeted for 10:50 a.m. ET and a backup at 10:24 a.m. ET on Monday, 30 November. It says this will be the ninth flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched KF-01, IMAP, NROL-77, GPS III-9, CRS-34, NROL-95, CRS-35 and one Starlink mission, that after stage separation the first stage will land on Landing Zone 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and that a live webcast will begin about 20 minutes prior to liftoff on the site and on X @SpaceX.
items.timeSource: Google News first listing of the official SpaceX mission page

items.title: Acquisition of Cursor (Anysphere) — 8-K
items.summary: An 8-K says SpaceX closed its acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor) on 14 Aug 2026, converting outstanding Cursor stock into 389,289,254 SpaceX Class A shares at an implied $60 billion equity value, plus 1,752,426 shares for vested RSUs before tax withholding. Unvested Cursor awards were assumed as about 29.1 million SpaceX RSUs and 44.4 million options, and the merger shares were issued in an unregistered Section 4(a)(2) transaction.
items.timeSource: EDGAR acceptance of the Cursor acquisition 8-K

items.title: SpaceX reports second quarter 2026 results
items.summary: SpaceX’s official second-quarter 2026 release reports revenue of $7.8 billion, up 92% from $4.1 billion, a net loss of $541 million, and Adjusted EBITDA of $3.5 billion. The letter highlights two Starship V3 flight tests in 90 days, $14.1 billion of contracted cloud-services sales, the announced $60 billion Cursor deal, 12.0 million Starlink consumer subscribers at $66 ARPU, $47.5 billion of backlog, and $100 billion of cash and marketable securities after the IPO.

items.summary: This 8-K furnishes SpaceX’s official second-quarter 2026 earnings release, the same document as the Q2 press item. The release reports $7.8 billion of revenue, a $541 million net loss, and $3.5 billion of Adjusted EBITDA.

items.title: SpaceX closes IPO, including full exercise of underwriters’ option
items.summary: SpaceX’s IR release says the IPO closed on 15 Jun 2026 with 638,888,888 Class A shares issued, including the full underwriters’ option for 83,333,333 extra shares, for about $85.7 billion of gross proceeds. Class A shares had begun trading on 12 Jun 2026 on the Nasdaq Global Select Market and Nasdaq Texas under the ticker SPCX.
items.timeSource: datePublished on the official IR release page

items.title: SpaceX prices IPO at $135.00 per share
items.summary: SpaceX priced 555,555,555 Class A shares at $135.00 and granted the underwriters a 30-day option to buy up to 83,333,333 more shares at the same price. The IR release said trading was expected to start on 12 Jun 2026 on Nasdaq Global Select and Nasdaq Texas under SPCX, with closing slated for 15 Jun 2026.
items.timeSource: datePublished on the official IR release page

items.title: SpaceX launches initial public offering roadshow
items.summary: SpaceX launched the IPO roadshow for 555,555,555 Class A shares, with an expected $135.00 offer price and the intended ticker SPCX on Nasdaq Global Select and Nasdaq Texas. The company also planned to grant underwriters a 30-day option for up to 83,333,333 additional shares.
